section_summary: This section continues an analysis of Japan’s debt, foreign exchange, and capacity to finance the war in China. Later documents examine Japanese bond sales in Hawaii, currency policy in occupied China, British credit to Japanese interests, and competing assessments of Japan’s financial vulnerability. The section ends with an embassy report and a newspaper text of Finance Minister Ishiwata’s 1939–40 budget speech.

subfiles.title: Analysis of Japan’s national debt and foreign debt service
subfiles.about: The concluding portion assesses Japan’s debt, bond financing, foreign exchange limits, and ability to service overseas obligations.
subfiles.summary: The report calculates funded debt and interest charges as of August 1938, then projects a steep increase in both if wartime bond issues continue. It attributes Japan’s initial financial resilience to material stocks, gold exports, restrained early war spending, and favorable export trade, all of which were weakening. Its conclusion weighs the incentives to maintain foreign debt service against scarce exchange and armament needs. A debt table and source list complete the report.

subfiles.title: Rumored British loan to Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew reports an unconfirmed rumor of a British loan to Japan and equal stabilization of the yen and Chinese dollar.
subfiles.summary: An American tobacco merchant relayed the rumor through Japanese representatives. Grew notes Japan’s concern about Chinese currency in Central China but says the embassy could not confirm a British loan.

subfiles.title: Reference to memorandum on Japan’s gold and foreign exchange
subfiles.from: Adviser on International Economic Affairs, Luthringer
subfiles.about: Points to a separately filed report on Japan’s gold and foreign exchange position, August 1–October 27, 1938.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to memorandum 894.5151/106.

subfiles.title: Possible unlawful sale of Japanese bonds in Hawaii
subfiles.from: William O. Douglas, Securities and Exchange Commission
subfiles.to: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Douglas reports an investigation into Japanese government bond sales in Hawaii under the Securities Act.
subfiles.summary: The commission sends an investigator to Honolulu and promises to advise the department of developments.

subfiles.title: Reply on Japanese bond sales in Hawaii
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Welles acknowledges the Hawaii investigation and recalls the commission’s handling of an earlier California case.
subfiles.summary: He assumes the commission will proceed in Hawaii along lines developed through earlier discussions with State Department officials.

subfiles.title: Hovey estate claim for missing Japanese bonds
subfiles.about: The Hovey estate’s attorney seeks State Department help obtaining replacement Imperial Japanese Government bonds.
subfiles.summary: Siegelstein says the Yokohama Specie Bank and Japanese authorities have not resolved the claim despite an offer of surety against double payment. He argues that the claim is against Japan’s government and requests action through diplomatic channels.

subfiles.title: Reply concerning the Hovey estate bonds
subfiles.from: Joseph R. Baker, Acting Legal Adviser
subfiles.about: The department asks for material facts and evidence of exhausted remedies before raising the Hovey claim with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Baker says the new letter adds no material information. He asks why the bank required a particular surety bond, why that surety refused, and what legal right supports the proposed substitute security.

subfiles.title: Bonuses into Bonds
subfiles.from: Charles H. Stephan, American Vice Consul, Nagoya
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: A Nagoya newspaper reports an Aichi plan to channel employees’ year-end bonuses into government bonds.
subfiles.summary: Stephan forwards a translation describing circulars to employers, schools, and municipalities, a special bond sale, and suggested purchase percentages by bonus size.

subfiles.title: Telephone conversation with William O. Douglas
subfiles.about: Hornbeck records State’s response to possible Securities and Exchange Commission action over Hawaii bond sales.
subfiles.summary: He told Douglas State did not expect to oppose injunction proceedings if the investigation warranted them.

subfiles.title: Routing instruction on commission correspondence
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck and Mr. Haiton
subfiles.about: The Under Secretary routes correspondence for an appropriate reply.
subfiles.summary: Directs Hornbeck and Haiton to prepare a reply.

subfiles.title: Commission’s position on Japanese bond sales in Hawaii
subfiles.about: Douglas contrasts apparently knowing violations in Hawaii with an earlier case stopped by warnings.
subfiles.summary: He says warnings may be insufficient in Hawaii and offers to consult before seeking an injunction.

subfiles.title: Reference to conversation on finances in Japan and China
subfiles.from: Adviser on International Economic Affairs, Luthringer
subfiles.about: Cross-reference to a memorandum of conversation with British financial advisers.
subfiles.summary: Identifies the participants and the memorandum’s subject.

subfiles.title: Financial conditions in Japan and China
subfiles.about: British financial advisers discuss Japanese currency control in China and capital flight from Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hall-Patch describes the Japanese army’s promotion of Federal Reserve Bank of North China notes, resistance by Chinese users and foreign powers, and potential exchange controls around Tientsin. He says Japanese yen circulating in China undermine exchange control and enable capital flight through Shanghai. Participants also discuss possible British-American exchange of information on Japanese capital movements and the financial condition of China.

subfiles.title: Visit to Osaka of Finance Minister and Bank of Japan Governor
subfiles.about: Reports speeches and business responses at Osaka banking and economic meetings.
subfiles.summary: Finance Minister Ikeda discusses gold shipments, deficits, bond absorption, state controls, and the coming budget; Bank of Japan Governor Yuki urges thrift. Osaka industrialists seek clearer controls, tax changes, credit for trade, and reliable raw materials. Discussion also covers the intended economic roles of Manchuria and China. The report concludes that business leaders support the government while fearing compulsory bond absorption and tighter controls.

subfiles.title: Introduction to analysis of Japan’s financial position
subfiles.about: Introduces a confidential analysis supplied by Arthur N. Young on Japan’s sensitivity to economic retaliation.
subfiles.summary: Corrected copy of telegram 46, section one.

subfiles.title: Introduction to analysis of Japan’s financial position
subfiles.about: Duplicates the introduction to Young’s digest of Japan’s finances.
subfiles.summary: Another copy of telegram 46, section one.

subfiles.title: Young’s view of economic retaliation against Japan
subfiles.about: Young favors restricting Japanese exports to Western markets as a way to reduce Japan’s import capacity.
subfiles.summary: He considers export restrictions more effective than restrictions limited to military supplies.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Chungking telegram 46
subfiles.about: Paraphrases the confidential financial analysis and Young’s proposed form of economic retaliation.
subfiles.summary: The paraphrase introduces a forthcoming digest of the analysis and explains Young’s preference for limiting imports from Japan in Western countries.

subfiles.title: Assessment of proposed economic retaliation against Japan
subfiles.about: Compares Chungking’s warning of Japanese financial vulnerability with a more resilient picture from Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: The writer points to growing Japanese domestic production and doubts that unilateral U.S. sanctions would exert decisive pressure. The memorandum proposes seeking Tokyo’s comments on the Chungking analysis.

subfiles.title: Digest of analysis of Japan’s financial position
subfiles.about: Transmits a confidential analysis of Japan’s balance of payments, raw material stocks, and gold reserves.
subfiles.summary: The digest describes falling foreign exchange earnings, a trade shift toward the yen bloc, a large external deficit, declining shipping receipts, and depleted material stocks. It says gold exports and tighter credit terms helped finance the 1938 deficit but could not be repeated indefinitely. It concludes that continued deficits could exhaust Japan’s gold reserves in 1939 and increase its vulnerability to coordinated economic pressure.

subfiles.title: Request for Tokyo’s comments on Chungking analysis
subfiles.about: Requests Tokyo’s comments on Chungking telegram 47 in light of the commercial attaché’s economic summary.
subfiles.summary: Asks the embassy to compare the two assessments.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of financial telegrams to Treasury
subfiles.about: Confidentially forwards telegrams from Chungking about Japan’s financial position.
subfiles.summary: Cover note enclosing Chungking financial reporting.

subfiles.title: Tokyo’s preliminary response to request for comments
subfiles.about: The embassy says it is studying Japan’s economic condition and will report its conclusions.
subfiles.summary: Grew promises a forthcoming assessment.

subfiles.title: Inquiry into British credits and sterling-yen exchange
subfiles.about: Requests discreet inquiry into British credits to Japanese interests and the sterling-yen peg.
subfiles.summary: Asks whether credits are secured by gold or other British bank deposits.

subfiles.title: British credits to Japan and mechanism of yen peg
subfiles.about: Reports reduced British credit to Japanese interests and the Yokohama Specie Bank’s role in supporting the yen.
subfiles.summary: Existing British credits have contracted since 1937, and new facilities would require security. The Yokohama Specie Bank’s London branch uses sterling and dollar assets, exchange certificates, and licensed yen sales to maintain the peg. The telegram also notes Rogers’s arrival in London, possibly concerning Chinese customs loans.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of London telegram 157
subfiles.about: Restates London’s findings on Japanese credit facilities and sterling-yen exchange operations.
subfiles.summary: The paraphrase describes the Yokohama Specie Bank’s dominant role in the London yen market and the sharp reduction in British short-term credit. It also mentions Rogers’s visit and the Chinese customs loans question.

subfiles.title: Response concerning Chinese customs loans
subfiles.about: Thanks the embassy for its credit report and invites information that arises on Chinese customs loans.
subfiles.summary: The department requests any readily available information about the loans.

subfiles.title: Request for updated report on British credits to Japan
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Joseph P. Kennedy, American Ambassador, London
subfiles.about: Requests an updated report on British commercial and banking credits to Japanese interests.
subfiles.summary: Seeks current information following London telegram 157.

subfiles.title: Tokyo cautions against firm conclusions on Japanese vulnerability
subfiles.about: The embassy says unknown material stocks make Chungking’s conclusion about economic retaliation speculative.
subfiles.summary: Grew promises a fuller report and says a clear, concise appraisal is impossible.

subfiles.title: Comment on Ishiwata’s Diet speech
subfiles.about: Comments on Tokyo despatch 3643 and the limits of Ishiwata’s optimistic budget interpretation.
subfiles.summary: Notes that postwar markets for expanded heavy industry remain uncertain.

subfiles.title: Speech of Finance Minister Sotaro Ishiwata before the 74th Diet
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports Ishiwata’s 1939–40 budget estimates, economic claims, and Japanese press responses.
subfiles.summary: The despatch outlines higher spending, taxes, and bond financing, with a separate military budget still to come. It reports Ishiwata’s confidence in savings, bond absorption, industrial expansion, and the yen peg. Grew also summarizes press doubts about the sterling link and observes that the favorable overall trade balance masks a large deficit with countries outside the yen bloc.

subfiles.title: Text of Finance Minister Ishiwata’s budget address
subfiles.about: Prints the substance of Ishiwata’s Diet address on Japan’s budget and wartime economic policy.
subfiles.summary: Ishiwata details proposed expenditures, tax increases, bond issues, savings and industrial investment, export promotion, foreign exchange policy, and gold mobilization. He calls for expanded productive capacity across Japan, Manchukuo, and China while maintaining controls on materials, prices, and consumption.
